voice_event.speaker: alx
voice_event.text: He was God's own Word, come to us in flesh - that is the whole of what we believed, and everything else grew from it. Our teachers used an old word for him: the Logos, God's reason and speech, the one through whom all things were made. Clement, one of our first teachers, called him the New Song: 'Behold the might of the new song! It has made men out of stones, men out of beasts'. He meant that the one who first set the world in order had come into it, to set people right. And near the end of our era, Athanasius put our whole hope in one sentence: 'He was made man that we might be made God'. Not that we become gods - but that his own life is opened to us and shared. If you want it in one line: the maker, come inside his making, to heal it.

voice_event.speaker: alx
voice_event.text: He entered human nature to heal it from within - not to teach or model, but to remake what sin had damaged. Athanasius put it plainly: by taking on our flesh, he trampled death down and opened resurrection life inside humanity itself. The doctor entered the sickness, as we said it. His death was not payment to satisfy a judge - it was the point where unbreakable divine life met human death and broke its hold. And his rising was that life let loose in flesh, so that everyone joined to him by baptism could share it. This was restoration, not rescue from outside: he repaired what the fall had broken, and carried it further than where it started. 'He was made man that we might be made God' - Athanasius's line captures the whole movement. What he did was join God's life to ours, permanently.

voice_event.speaker: alx
voice_event.text: God's own Word and reason, through whom all things were made. The word came to us from the Greeks - they used it for the rational principle that holds the cosmos together - but we put it to a use it had never had. We named the Word who had become flesh. This was not wordplay. When we said Logos, we meant the one through whom the Father made everything, who is never separate from him, who speaks in Scripture, and who entered human nature in Jesus. Clement called him the New Song that set the world in tune. Athanasius said he was made man that we might be made God. The Logos is the center that makes Scripture, learning, worship, and the soul's own change one movement rather than four separate things. God's reason, God's speech, God himself - and ours, when we are joined to him.

glosses.plain_meaning: Not first a name for the Bible. The eternal Word who speaks - who made everything, and now speaks to the soul through Scripture too.
glosses.quick_meaning: Not a name for the Bible - the eternal Word who speaks, including through Scripture.
glosses.translational_sense: Isn't "the Word of God" just another name for the Bible? This world heard something behind the book: the eternal Word who spoke creation into being and now speaks through this text - the person, not the page, is what gives Scripture its power to change someone.
false_friend: an ancient document with religious authority

glosses.plain_meaning: Scripture is not a historical record of what God once said - it is the Logos speaking now, through the text, to a soul formed to hear.
glosses.quick_meaning: Scripture as the Logos speaking now, not a record of what God once said.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Isn't reading the Bible just interpreting an old text correctly?' - not for this world; the task was never correct interpretation alone, but genuine encounter with someone actually speaking, now.
false_friend: a set of fixed propositions to be believed
a collection of ancient documents to be analyzed

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: alx
voice_event.text: We believed it because we heard it in Scripture, we received it from the apostles, and we saw it doing what it claimed to do. The first Christians handed down baptism, the bread and cup, the teaching, and the faith itself - we did not make these up in Alexandria, we kept what had been given. And Scripture itself named him the Word: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.' That was not our invention; it was the text we read aloud every week. But there is a second reason, harder to prove and just as real. We saw lives changed. The martyrs went to their deaths without fear - Athanasius said their contempt for death was the risen Christ's continuing signature. Students like Gregory came in wanting philosophy and left with their whole direction turned toward God. We believed it because it worked: souls were actually remade, and we could see it.

citations.sentence: We believed it because we heard it in Scripture, we received it from the apostles, and we saw it doing what it claimed to do.
